summary: Describes how forward error correction codes can efficiently provide or augment reliability for one-to-many multicast transport. A key advantage is that the same repair packets can fix different loss patterns at different receivers. It describes classes of codes and some of their basic properties.

plainLanguage.summary: If many people each miss different pieces of a message, one set of extra repair pieces can help all of them at once. This note explains why that works.

questions: forward error correction multicast loss repair
subtitle: Why sending extra coded repair packets lets one multicast sender fix different losses at many receivers at once.

tldr.problem: Retransmission requests (ARQ) scale poorly to very many receivers, and a data carousel makes receivers wait a full round to recover one lost packet.
tldr.mechanism: FEC erasure codes turn k source symbols into encoding symbols so that any k (or slightly more) received symbols rebuild the object. The same repair packet therefore helps every receiver, whatever it lost.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes simple, small block, large block and expandable codes, how to name symbols in packets, and how to handle variable-length symbols. It is an Informational overview, not a protocol.

facts.label: Ideal recovery
facts.value: any k of the encoding symbols

today: RFC 3453 is an Informational document and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It serves as background on FEC terminology and code families for reliable multicast, and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why FEC for Reliable Multicast
sections.content:
The usual way to make transport reliable is ARQ, where receivers send requests for retransmission over a back channel. It works well one-to-one, as TCP shows. For one-to-very-many it suffers from feedback implosion, needs a back channel, and wastes bandwidth and time when receivers lost different packets.

Where there is little or no back channel, such as satellite transmission, a Data Carousel is sometimes used: the sender splits the object into equal pieces called source symbols and cycles through them. A receiver that loses a packet must wait an entire round to see it again.

Forward Error Correction (FEC) can augment or replace these methods. In multicast the network or transport layers already discard corrupted packets, so FEC is used mainly as an erasure code, recovering lost packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking the teacher to repeat things does not work if a hundred kids all ask at once. Reading the whole list again and again makes you wait for the part you missed.

sections.title: Source Symbols, Encoding Symbols and Overhead
sections.content:
An FEC encoder takes k equal-length source symbols and produces encoding symbols of the same length, placed in packets with enough information to identify them. Ideally the decoder can rebuild all k source symbols from any k encoding symbols.

  • Block codes take k source symbols and a number n and produce n encoding symbols. A systematic encoder sends the k source symbols plus n-k redundant ones.
  • Expandable codes generate as many unique encoding symbols as asked for, on demand, in the same time per symbol.
  • Reception overhead is how much more than k symbols are needed. If k*(1+ep) are needed, the overhead is ep*100%; for example k*1.05 symbols means 5%.
  • Small codes are efficient for small k, large codes for much larger k.

The payoff is that one repair packet is fully useful to every receiver, regardless of its past losses, which can raise scalability by orders of magnitude.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a puzzle where any ten pieces from a bag of twelve rebuild the picture. It does not matter which two you are missing.

sections.title: How Protocols Use FEC
sections.content:
The RFC sketches three patterns.

  • FEC plus ARQ. Send all source symbols of all blocks, have receivers report how many symbols they lack per block, then send as many redundant symbols per block as the maximum missing at any receiver. Those symbols help every receiver missing something in that block.
  • FEC Data Carousel. With a large block code, the sender cycles through the n encoding symbols of the object. A receiver can join at any time and recover as long as it gets at least k symbols during the next n. With block codes applied per block, symbols from different blocks should be interleaved. Expandable codes never repeat packets, so any k are enough.
  • One-shot transmission. The sender decides in advance how many encoding symbols to send, and each is sent at most once, which suits streaming where the stream is cut into objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Either ask everyone what they missed and send the right helper pieces, or keep sending fresh helper pieces forever so anyone can join late and still finish.

sections.title: The Families of FEC Codes
sections.content:
Simple codes. One XOR parity symbol protects against a single loss. For source symbols a, b, c and d the redundant symbol is e = a XOR b XOR c XOR d, and any missing one is the XOR of the rest. Row and column parity over a square grid can also be used, but such constructions come nowhere near the ideal any-k-of-n behavior.

Small block codes. A block (n, k) code needs any k of n symbols, with no reception overhead. Reed-Solomon codes are a popular example. Values of k and n must be small (for example below 256) because larger ones make encoding and decoding too expensive, so longer objects are split into source blocks.

Large block codes. Tornado codes allow k in the tens of thousands with n restricted to a small multiple of k, such as n = 2k. They need slightly more than k symbols; the RFC cites a 5-10% reception overhead for that case. Packets are sent in a random order.

Expandable codes. LT codes make each encoding symbol randomly and independently from a random encoding symbol ID, so they can be generated by multiple senders. The RFC cites a reception overhead under 5% for k in the tens to hundreds of thousands.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest trick is one extra card that is the sum of all the others, which fixes one lost card. Fancier recipes fix many losses, either for small piles or for very big piles of cards.

sections.title: Naming Symbols and Variable-Length Symbols
sections.content:
Each packet must say which encoding symbols it carries. For block codes this can be a block number plus an encoding symbol ID made of an encoding flag (1 for a source symbol, 0 for a redundant one) and a source or redundant symbol ID. An alternative numbers source symbols 0 to k-1 and redundant symbols k to n-1. For LT codes the block number and a random encoding symbol ID (for example 32 bits) identify each symbol.

Block FEC codes need equal-length symbols, so the RFC gives a technique for variable-length ones. Pad each symbol with zeroes up to the maximum length lmax, and prepend its true length in x bytes, a protocol constant. All padded symbols then have length x+lmax. A receiver can tell a block is variable-length because redundant symbols are longer than the source symbols, and it recovers each original length from the first x bytes after decoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet needs a label saying which piece it is. If the pieces are different sizes, you pad the short ones with blanks and write down their real size first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
FEC adds no security concerns beyond sending the same data without it. A malicious sender can still inject corrupted encoding symbols. If a receiver accepts them it may rebuild a corrupted object, which application-level authentication can detect but only by discarding the whole transfer, an effective denial of service.

The RFC suggests screening source addresses against a list of authentic senders, noting that addresses can be spoofed, and having transport protocols offer robust per-symbol source authentication. It recommends a packet authentication scheme such as TESLA together with FEC, so unauthenticated packets are discarded and the object is still recovered from authentic ones.
sections.plainLanguage: If a prankster slips in fake puzzle pieces, your picture comes out wrong. So you should check that each piece really came from the teacher.
